title: Air India Launches Course-by-Course Fine Dining in Business Class on UK Routes
excerpt: Linen tables, individually plated courses and Vista Verve tableware replace the tray on India-UK flights first, with A350, 787-9 and 777-300 routes to follow.
body:
• Air India launched multicourse, course-by-course fine dining in Business Class on October 22, 2026, starting on India–UK flights to London Heathrow, London Gatwick and Birmingham.
  • What changes: no single tray — linen-covered tables, individually plated appetisers, mains and desserts, dedicated Vista Verve tableware and a Martaban-inspired cruet set, served at your own pace.
  • Rollout: the service will expand progressively to other long-haul and ultra-long-haul routes on Airbus A350, Boeing 787-9 and Boeing 777-300 aircraft; no dates for US routes have been announced.
  • Reader utility: if you are booking Business Class between India and the UK now, you get the new service; for US–India flights, check your aircraft type and book on Air India's US booking page — the upgrade has not yet been confirmed for those routes.

Air India has replaced the Business Class meal tray with a restaurant-style, course-by-course service on its longest flights. The airline announced the multicourse fine dining launch on October 22, starting with flights between India and the United Kingdom — London Heathrow, London Gatwick and Birmingham — and said it will expand progressively across its long-haul network.

What is served, and how

The change is primarily about presentation, sequencing and pace, according to both the airline's release and Live From A Lounge's detailed breakdown. Crew set a linen-covered table and bring each course on its own plate: appetisers first, then the main course, then dessert and cheese, with dedicated tableware for each. Passengers eat at their preferred pace rather than on the galley's schedule.

https://x.com/airindia/status/2113162244670509324

The new Vista Verve tableware collection includes separate plates for appetisers, mains, snacks, dessert and cheese, a signature glass and a specially designed espresso cup. Its centrepiece is a cruet set shaped like a Martaban, the traditional Indian storage jar used to preserve flavours and family recipes — a deliberate nod to Indian homes inside a contemporary cabin.

On food itself, the release points to refreshed menus, an award-winning wine selection and enhanced tea service, building on the global menu Air India introduced earlier — Awadhi-inspired dishes, Japanese Teppanyaki bowls, chicken bibimbap and home-style options such as masala dal khichdi, as detailed in the airline's official menu press release (PDF). Live From A Lounge notes highlighted dishes from that broader menu include Awadhi vegetarian and non-vegetarian meals and contemporary Pan-Asian options, and reports that London catering has switched to DO & CO, the premium airline caterer, at Heathrow and Gatwick.

"The introduction of our fine dining-style, course-by-course meal service in Business Class is another step in our broader Air India transformation journey, creating a globally benchmarked premium travel experience while remaining rooted in the warmth and authenticity of Indian hospitality."

— Rajesh Dogra, Chief Customer Experience Officer, Air India

Which flights get it first

For now, only India–UK Business Class. Air India says the service will be progressively extended to other international long-haul and ultra-long-haul routes operated by its Airbus A350, Boeing 787-9 and Boeing 777-300 aircraft. It has not named the next routes or given dates, and it has said nothing about First Class or Premium Economy in this announcement.

That sequencing matters for diaspora travellers. The UK is one of Air India's most competitive premium markets, where it faces rivals with long-established restaurant-style dining. US–India nonstops — the routes most readers of this publication fly — use the same aircraft types named for the expansion, which makes them logical candidates, but until Air India confirms them, travellers should not assume the new service on a New York, San Francisco or Chicago departure.

The test is consistency

Live From A Lounge raises the central question plainly: a multicourse service needs more crew time and coordination than a tray, must be balanced against sleep on overnight flights, and must taste as good as it looks after food has been prepared, chilled, loaded and reheated. A polished service on one flight and a rushed one on the next will not build confidence in premium fares.

The dining upgrade sits inside Air India's wider transformation: new A350s and 787-9s joining the fleet, legacy aircraft being retrofitted with new cabins, and repeated investments in menus, wine and tea. For Business Class passengers flying India–UK this winter, the upgrade is immediate and tangible. Bookings for those routes are on Air India's official site, where you can also check aircraft type for onward long-haul sectors before you pay a premium fare for a service that has not yet reached that route.
